original_question: Is it consistent that ℵω is the only breaking point in the positive spectrum of strong polarized relations? More generally, can the continuum c be arbitrarily large while the only breaking points in that spectrum are exactly the cardinals of countable cofinality?
target_in_paper: Problem 2.15 in Section 2 (Countable problems), read together with the immediate setup in Problems 2.13–2.14 and the background criterion in Theorem 1.6. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s official formulation: it correctly singles out ℵω, uses the paper’s own breaking-point language, and matches the more general clause about arbitrarily large 𝔠 and countable-cofinality breaking points. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))
missing_details: The paper’s problem is specifically about the countable polarized relation, with the small component fixed to ω, not about arbitrary polarized pairs. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))

The relevant positive spectrum is the set of uncountable cardinals κ with ℵ1 ≤ κ ≤ 𝔠 such that binom{κ}{ω} → binom{κ}{ω}^{1,1}_2 holds; this ambient interval is supplied by Problems 2.13 and 2.14 and is implicit in Problem 2.15. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))

To make the question stand-alone, the strong polarized notation should be unpacked: every coloring d: κ×ω → 2 must admit A ⊆ κ and B ⊆ ω with |A| = κ and |B| = ω such that d is constant on A×B. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))

The term breaking point is informal in the paper and should be made explicit as a failure point of that spectrum; the sentence before Problem 2.15 identifies ℵω as such a point because binom{ℵω}{ω} ↛ binom{ℵω}{ω}^{1,1}_2. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))
The general clause is about which κ ≤ 𝔠 fail the countable strong polarized relation, not about all cardinals in the universe. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))

The nearby motivation uses Theorem 1.6: below the splitting number 𝔰, positivity holds exactly when cf(κ) ≠ ω, which explains why the paper asks whether countable-cofinality cardinals are precisely the breaking points. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))
refined_question: Is it consistent with ZFC that, for the countable strong polarized spectrum S = { κ : ℵ1 ≤ κ ≤ 𝔠 and binom{κ}{ω} → binom{κ}{ω}^{1,1}_2 }, one has S = { κ : ℵ1 ≤ κ ≤ 𝔠 and κ ≠ ℵω }; more generally, can 𝔠 be arbitrarily large with S = { κ : ℵ1 ≤ κ ≤ 𝔠 and cf(κ) > ω }? Here binom{κ}{ω} → binom{κ}{ω}^{1,1}_2 means that every coloring d: κ×ω → 2 admits A ⊆ κ and B ⊆ ω with |A| = κ and |B| = ω such that d is constant on A×B.
justification: The draft clearly targets Problem 2.15, not the background theorems in Section 1: the wording about ℵω as the only breaking point and about arbitrarily large 𝔠 with countable-cofinality breaking points is exactly the paper’s wording. I only sharpened it by making explicit the ambient spectrum and the arrow notation, because the paper leaves positive spectrum and breaking point informal and relies on surrounding Problems 2.13–2.14, Definition 0.1, and Theorem 1.6 for that context. I did not broaden the problem to uncountable small components, other polarized pairs, or later large-cardinal questions. ([shelah.logic.at](https://shelah.logic.at/files/178125/1012.pdf))
